title: Control Plane for User Experiences
content:
One-pager (working draft) — internal brief: why Redwood should lead with the "inference control plane" as a product narrative that ties developer velocity, UX reliability, and unit economics together.

Context / why this doc exists:
- We keep pitching Redwood around infrastructure features (dedicated, private, kernel optimizations). That resonates with infra teams but doesn’t directly connect to product and growth teams who own end-user experience.
- Hypothesis: framing Redwood as the control plane that guarantees predictable user experiences (latency, consistency, cost predictability, graceful degradation) gives us a clearer buyer story for PMs and platform leads.

Mission line (candidate):
Redwood is the control plane for dependable LLM-powered experiences — making product teams confident that their features behave the same in the lab and in production.

Core thesis (concise):
- Models change, hardware changes, traffic patterns change. What must not change is the customer experience.
- The competitive lever for product teams isn’t owning the model; it’s controlling the signals that determine the live experience: latency SLOs, quality regression protection, and predictable unit cost.
- Redwood provides that control plane: a single API and operations surface that unifies routing, caching, fallback, and capacity so teams ship and scale with predictable outcomes.

Problem framing (for GTM):
- PM / product engineering pain: Features break at scale — hallucinations spike during bursts, latency variability kills conversion, model rollouts cause regressions.
- Platform/infra pain: Customers are asked to stitch together autoscaling, cache layers, fallbacks, and monitoring — fragile and expensive.
- Business pain: Unpredictable token spend, surprise incidents, and poor SLAs create churn risk.

Promise (one-sentence):
Deliver consistent LLM experiences across environments so product teams can own outcomes, not infrastructure.

Proof points (what we can point to quickly):
- Predictable latency: continuous batching + smart routing reduces P95 tail by X% vs unmanaged endpoints (internal benchmark references: JIRA-INF-842).
- Cost guardrails: Optimize recommends batching/quantization profiles that reduced customer A's per-token spend 3x on retrieval-heavy traffic (anecdote — needs permission to quote).
- Rollouts that don’t regress: canary + automatic fallback to verified model variant cut regression windows from days to hours during a pilot.

Differentiators (short bullets):
- Experience SLOs first: SLAs and tooling oriented around UX metrics (latency, correctness signals, error budgets), not just throughput.
- Unified control plane: single policy layer for routing, cache, and fallbacks across hosted, dedicated, private.
- Operational opinionation: prebuilt policies (latency-first, cost-first, quality-safeguard) so teams get sensible defaults and can customize.
- Observability designed for regressions: prompt-set-linked alerts and traceable token-cost lineage in Console.

Audience-specific snippets (elevator pitches):
- To an engineering manager: "We reduce incident surface and mean time to mitigate by standardizing how requests are routed, cached, and downgraded across models — fewer surprises in production."
- To a product manager: "Ship features that behave the same for 10 users and 10M users — we protect your UX with canaries, quality checks, and graceful fallbacks."
- To a platform lead: "Get a policy-driven control plane that enforces SLOs across business units while giving each team fast self-serve endpoints."

Top objections and rebuttals (prep for sales):
- "We can just build this ourselves": Rebuttal — yes, but rebuilding reliable routing + caching + quality monitoring is 6-12 months of infra debt and ongoing ops cost. We offer production-hardened primitives that integrate with existing infra and reduce TCO.
- "We control our models in-house": Rebuttal — model control is necessary but insufficient; model behavior at scale depends on deployment topology, caching, and request routing — we standardize that so model ownership becomes less risky.
- "Latency-sensitive workloads prefer in-house infra": Rebuttal — Redwood offers Dedicated and Private deployment modes and hardware-aware routing with verified performance profiles to meet strict latency SLOs.

Suggested primary headline for marketing: "Make LLM features behave the same in production as they do in tests."
Secondary headline options: "A control plane for predictable AI UX"; "From model to experience: control the last mile of LLM features."

Calls-to-action / pilot offers for GTM:
- 30-day Experience SLA pilot: dedicated capacity + rollout plan + custom canary, with success metrics defined up front.
- Engineer workshop: runbook + config labs for teams to migrate one endpoint and measure P95 and cost delta.

Open questions / risks (notes):
- Need to agree on a single measurable set of "experience SLOs" we will champion externally (latency P95, percent of responses within fallback, cost per 1k queries). Proposal: latency P50/P95, regression-rate (per prompt set), and cost-per-1k. (ACTION: product/metrics to define exact formulas).
- Legal/compliance callouts when using customer prompt-sets for alerting — need legal review. (Linked: CONFLUENCE-1234).
- Customer proof: identify 2 customers willing to be named case studies for pilot. (ACTION: CS outreach, owner Miguel Torres).

Launch checklist (required assets):
- One-pager (finalized) for sales — highlight pilot, technical hooks, ROI example.
- 1-slide technical primer for platform/infra reviewers.
- Runbook template + sample canary configs for Console.
- Landing page copy and 2 short engineer-focused blog posts.

Operational notes (internal):
- Slack thread to centralize discussion: #g2m-experience-control (started 2025-11-09).
- Jira epic: JIRA-INF-842 -> create child stories: case-study outreach, metrics page update, pilot onboarding flow.

Rough next steps (short timeline):
- Week 0-2: agree on SLO definitions + finalize core messaging (this doc -> finalize).
- Week 2-6: validate with 2 platform/customer partners and build pilot onboarding.
- Week 6-12: create assets, train sales, launch pilot offers.

Notes-to-self / brain dump (informal):
- Keep the phrasing practical: talk about conversion, retention, and engineering hours saved — PMs care about user impact, CFO cares about predictable spend.
- Avoid technical fetishization of kernels/quantization in external messaging unless the audience is infra. Frame those as levers that feed the control plane.
- Potential tagline experiment: "Control the last mile of AI experiences."
